name: Career Studies
subject: Guidance and Career Education
description: This course gives students the opportunity to develop the skills, knowledge, and habits that will support them in their education and career/life planning. Students will learn about global work trends, and seek opportunities within the school and community to expand and strengthen their transferable skills and their ability to adapt to the changing world of work. On the basis of exploration, reflective practice, and decision-making processes, students will make connections between their skills, interests, and values and their postsecondary options, whether in apprenticeship training, college, community living, university, or the workplace. They will set goals and create a plan for their first postsecondary year. As part of their preparation for the future, they will learn about personal financial management – including the variety of saving and borrowing tools available to them and how to use them to their advantage – and develop a budget for their first year after secondary school.

elaborations.text:
Strategies to help manage stress and promote balance: maintaining health routines, such as getting sufficient sleep, going outside, and participating in physical activity; developing and maintaining healthy eating practices; making it a habit to reserve time for self-reflection; connecting with nature; taking a break from technology; journalling; listening to music; doing mindful breathing or visualization exercises; making a list of priorities; developing a plan of action; using time-management strategies; connecting with a mentor, friend, family member, or trusted adult; participating in group or community activities; participating in spiritual or cultural activities; volunteering
  Signs that could indicate stress is becoming problematic: Changes in thoughts: falling into “thinking traps”, such as all-or-none thinking, catastrophizing, jumping to conclusions, and overgeneralizing; increased sensitivity to criticism; persistent negative thoughts about oneself, others, or the future; thoughts of self-harm or suicide; Changes in emotions: feeling worried all the time; persistent sadness; sense of helplessness, hopelessness, or worthlessness; frequent fluctuations in mood; feeling overwhelmed and unable to keep up with demands; increased physical discomforts, such as stomachaches or headaches; Changes in actions: withdrawal from family and friends; avoidance of school, work, or social activities; decline in school or work performance; unusual irritability, aggression, or defiance in interactions with others; frequent crying; changes in eating practices or sleeping patterns; increased need to seek approval and validation; increased use of caffeine, alcohol, nicotine or other substances; self-harm behaviours

elaborations.text:
We all feel stress at times and some stress can be helpful in our lives. A moderate level of stress can help motivate us and enhance our focus, alertness, and performance, especially in tasks that require attention and concentration, such as taking a test or preparing for a job interview. We can also develop new skills and grow as individuals when we try new things in a safe and appropriate environment. Can you think of a situation where stress helped you?
  We cannot always choose when and how we experience stress, but we can choose how we prepare for and respond to stress in our lives. We can be intentional about developing healthy coping strategies and incorporating them into our routines. We can develop a habit of mind for managing stress by practicing these strategies regularly, in both stressful and non-stressful situations. Can you think of different strategies that might work at different times or in different circumstances?
  How are physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual health related? Why is it important to understand the links between our body, mind, emotion, and spirit? Are there spiritual or cultural practices that support you in times of stress or challenge?
  What can you learn from various First Nations, Métis, and Inuit and other holistic approaches to mental health and wellness to navigate towards balance?
  We all have days that can feel challenging but sometimes we get stuck feeling a certain way and our strategies to manage stress do not seem to help as much as they usually do. When this happens, we can experience strong feelings that may become long-lasting and have a negative impact on our lives. They may get in the way of schoolwork, friendships, family events, or activities we usually enjoy. When this happens, it can be a sign that we may be experiencing a mental health problem and need additional support or need to make a change in our lives. What are the early signs and changes that you might notice when stress is starting to negatively impact your day-to-day functioning? What changes might you notice in the way you are thinking, feeling, or acting?

It is important to keep in mind that students may already have healthy ways of supporting their mental health based on personal, family, cultural, and community strengths. Teachers can encourage students to explore a variety of additional strategies and to think critically and intentionally about what works for them. Teachers can reinforce that not all strategies are appropriate or effective for everyone or in every circumstance.
  Teachers can support students in understanding that, in situations where stress is more complex and potentially difficult to navigate, seeking support from trusted adults is essential. It is important that students understand that they are not expected to use individual strategies to adjust or adapt to circumstances involving racism or marginalization.
  Teachers can co-create a learning environment with students and communities that includes resources that promote the use of various mental health strategies and respect students as complex individuals with diverse needs. This type of environment can invite a variety of strength-based approaches and can be responsive to the unique challenges and needs of all students. When considering resources, teachers can incorporate the voices and experiences of all students, including those from historically marginalized communities, so that students can explore what might be relevant and helpful for them.

elaborations.text:
Deciding to take action and reach out for support when you notice that you are struggling with your mental health is an important first step in taking care of yourself. There are people in your circle who care and want you to be well. You can start a conversation with a trusted adult by saying “Something has been bothering me. Do you have a few minutes?” or “I’ve been feeling really stressed lately and I’m not sure what to do about it.” In what other ways could you let someone know that you need support with your mental health?
  When someone is struggling with their mental health, they may turn to you as a friend for support. You can listen, share resources, and try to identify who might be helpful in these circumstances. However, being a supportive friend is not a substitute for professional help. You should encourage your friend to seek assistance from mental health professionals, and, if you are concerned about your friend, tell a trusted adult. If you need support, who are the trusted adults that you would reach out to? In addition to recommending professional help, what else can you do to support a friend who is struggling with their mental health?
  We are all unique and the strategies that we find helpful and who we choose to talk to will be different for each one of us. For example, some people, including those living in remote or rural communities, may find that digital supports, such as Health811, are easier and faster to access than in-person support. It is a good idea to consider a range of strategies and resources, and to try and figure out which ones work best for you. It is also important to keep seeking help until you get the help you need and to recognize that feeling better may take time. If you are feeling unsure or overwhelmed by the choices available, who can help you navigate access to support that works for you?

strands.title: Exploring and Preparing for the World of Work
strands.describer: By the end of this course, students will:

overall_expectations.title: Exploring Work Trends and the Importance of Transferable Skills
overall_expectations.describer: By the end of this course, students will:
overall_expectations.text: demonstrate an understanding, based on research, of a variety of local and global trends related to work and employment, including the effect some of those trends have had on workers’ rights and responsibilities and on the role of transferable skills in career development today
overall_expectations.text_html: demonstrate an understanding, based on research, of a variety of local and global trends related to work and employment, including the effect some of those trends have had on workers’ rights and responsibilities and on the role of transferable skills in career development today

specific_expectations.text: identify some recent and evolving technological, economic, and social trends that have influenced the world of work, both locally and globally, noting their impact on the kind of work we do and how we do it as well as on workers’ rights and responsibilities, and analyse the possible impact of those trends on their own choices now and in the future
specific_expectations.text_html: identify some recent and evolving technological, economic, and social trends that have influenced the world of work, both locally and globally, noting their impact on the kind of work we do and how we do it as well as on workers’ rights and responsibilities, and analyse the possible impact of those trends on their own choices now and in the future

elaborations.text:
Trends that affect the work we do: the growth of automation, robotics, artificial intelligence, and new digital technologies, which has brought about a wide range of changes, including: increasing opportunities in STEM fields (science, technology, engineering, mathematics), technological advancements in industries such as manufacturing and the agri-food industry, growing demand for highly skilled workers who perform “knowledge-intensive tasks” and for skilled tradespeople familiar with new technologies; globalization, which has created a growing demand for remote workers all over the world who bring strong communication and collaborative skills to team-based global projects; significant social changes, such as an aging population and the retirement of many current workers, which has led to increased opportunities in health care and support service jobs 
  Trends that are changing how we work: the growth of platform economies, which has increased opportunities for entrepreneurship and eliminated a variety of traditional jobs; a wider acceptance of the need for work/life balance, which has led to greater opportunities for telecommuting, flexible hours, and compressed work weeks, as well as parental (maternity and/or paternity) leave; a shift to a more balanced workforce that recognizes and values the importance of equity, diversity, and inclusion, which has led to greater opportunities for a diverse population, including people who may require assistive devices or special supports in order to participate fully in the workplace 
  Trends that have influenced workers’ rights and responsibilities: the growth of short-term work opportunities and the gig economy, which has resulted in fewer “jobs for life” and fewer protections but more opportunities to “be your own boss”, leading to changes in employment standards and in the rights and responsibilities of workers
elaborations.text_html:

elaborations.text:
Different forms of borrowing: federal student loans; provincial student loans, such as those available through the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP); loans or bursaries from their local communities; personal (unsecured) loans from a bank or credit union; lines of credit; credit cards; overdrafts; understanding the pros and cons of various types of loans; payday loans 

Risks and benefits: use of a credit card can improve an individual’s credit rating, but a poor credit rating will result from failure to comply with payment conditions; student or bank loans can enable a person to pay for a costly item, such as tuition or a vehicle, in instalments, but too much debt can lead to a poor credit rating or even bankruptcy; borrowing from friends or family can be convenient because of more flexible repayment terms, but if the loan is not repaid this could have a negative effect on a personal relationship
